# LLM-as-judge: model-based grading of AI agent outputs

A distinct cross-source theme is using an LLM as a judge or grader to evaluate output quality, in contrast to deterministic checks. Multiple sources describe LLM-as-judge scoring followed by a rubric, note the need for calibration against human experts, and advise guarding against non-determinism and hallucination in judges. This distillation gathers the shared practices and caveats around model-based evaluation.

## LLM-as-judge scoring against a rubric

Sources describe using a language model to grade responses against explicit criteria (a rubric), and treating these judges as reliable only when the rubric is well-defined and anchored with examples.

- Heltweg uses LLM-as-judge: AI agents score answers per a defined rubric, and he states that with good prompts LLMs are 'reliable judges' of response quality, but the rubrics can be adjusted when judge judgments don't match the domain expert's; he defines annotations in Markdown with definitions, rating scales, and anchor examples, using a five-point Likert scale with score plus reasoning.
- Anthropic's evals post categorizes model-based grading as rubric scoring, natural-language assertions, pairwise comparison, reference-based eval, and multi-judge consensus, and describes these as flexible, scalable, and nuanced but non-deterministic, more expensive, and requiring calibration with human graders.
- Anthropic's tools post uses a verifier 'as simple as exact string comparison or as advanced as having Claude judge responses', while cautioning against overly strict verifiers that reject valid alternative answers.
- Anthropic's evals post also stresses calibration: calibrate LLM-as-judge with human experts, give LLM judges a 'way out' (a return 'Unknown' option) to avoid hallucination, and use isolated judges per evaluation dimension.
- Osmani advocates 'LLM-as-a-Judge' for subjective acceptance criteria, alongside self-verification prompts, in his spec-writing framework.

Sources: [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md](../summaries/how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md)

## Limits and calibration of model-based judges

Sources warn that LLM judges are not perfect: they can be non-deterministic, may hallucinate, and can fail to capture expert nuance, so human calibration and domain knowledge are essential.

- Heltweg emphasizes domain knowledge is essential for good annotation: one annotation per quality dimension with clear descriptions and examples for every scale point, and notes judge judgments may not match the domain expert's, requiring rubric adjustment.
- Anthropic's evals post reports that Opus 4.5 scored 42% on CORE-Bench rising to 95% after fixing rigid grading, ambiguous specs, and irreproducible stochastic tasks — showing that judge-based and deterministic grading both carry subtle bugs.
- Anthropic's tools post notes that evaluation agents don't necessarily know correct answers, and that what agents omit can be more important than what they include ('LLMs don't always say what they mean').
- Coyle's ontology-as-guardrail proposal is an alternative/complement to judge-based scoring: instead of (or in addition to) an LLM judging quality, use a formal ontology-based validator to check that an agent's response or proposed action is reasonable before it executes.
- Anthropic's evals post describes how human studies (SME review, inter-annotator agreement) are the gold standard and should be reserved for calibrating LLM graders and evaluating subjective outputs.

Sources: [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [why-agentic-systems-need-ontologies-frank-coyle-uc-berkeley.md](../summaries/why-agentic-systems-need-ontologies-frank-coyle-uc-berkeley.md)

# Measuring AI agents: evals, baselines, and regression-style testing

A strong cross-source theme is the systematic evaluation of AI agents and workflows through evals, baselines, and regression-style testing, adapted from traditional software testing. Sources argue 'you cannot improve what you cannot measure,' recommend building offline datasets and baselines before changes, and emphasize iterating on test quality and reading transcripts rather than trusting raw scores. This distillation synthesizes the evals workflow across the sources concerned with measurement.

## Measurable baselines and regression testing for agents

Sources converge on applying a testing/measurement mindset to agents: establish a baseline, build a dataset, then continuously evaluate against it so changes or model switches do not silently regress quality.

- Heltweg's core argument adapts software regression testing to AI: 'you cannot improve what you cannot measure' — define how to measure current output quality, set a baseline, then build an automated pipeline to evaluate against that baseline continuously, catching regressions whenever you make changes or switch models.

# Prompts and specs as code: treating agent engineering as a software engineering discipline

A prominent cross-source theme is that building reliable AI agents and prompt/spec systems should be treated as a software engineering discipline rather than ad hoc experimentation. Several sources converge on treating prompts and specifications as code, structuring files (JSON for structured data, Markdown for prose) as durable state, and version-controlling specifications and workflows. This distillation captures the framing, the file-based state pattern, iterative maintenance, and the limits acknowledged by the authors.

## Prompts and specs as code, executed on an unreliable computer

Multiple authors reframe writing prompts for LLM coding agents as a form of 'metaprogramming' or engineering practice, mapping traditional software concepts onto prompt-driven execution so that behavior becomes deterministic and revisable.

- Mario Zechner's core thesis is that 'agentic engineering' is usually ad hoc experimentation; he recommends treating LLMs as 'an extremely slow kind of unreliable computer that we program with natural language,' mapping Program = the prompt, Inputs = prepared info/user input/tool outputs, State = data serialized to disk (JSON for structured data via jq, Markdown for unstructured), and Outputs = generated code/diffs/summaries.
- Addy Osmani frames a good AI-agent spec as a 'source of truth' document that should be a living, version-controlled artifact and an 'executable artifact' integrated into toolchains, blending PRD and SRS mindsets.
- Osmani argues agents need context broken into modular prompts rather than one giant prompt, citing the 'curse of instructions' — research that piling more instructions into a prompt drops model adherence — and recommends dividing specs into phases/components with per-section summaries as a hierarchical index.
- Karpathy's schema layer (e.g., CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md) plays the analogous role of a config/instruction file that makes a language model a 'disciplined maintainer rather than a generic chatbot', and he describes it as co-evolved over time.
- Anthropic's evals post makes the same engineering-discipline point at the team level: teams without evals stay in reactive debugging loops, and rigorous evals become necessary once agents scale and 'fly blind'.

Sources: [prompts-are-code-json-md-files-are-state.md](../summaries/prompts-are-code-json-md-files-are-state.md), [how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md](../summaries/how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md), [llm-wiki-github.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-github.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md)

## Files as state: JSON and Markdown as the durable medium

A consistent implementation pattern across sources is persisting state and knowledge in plain files — structured data in JSON, prose in Markdown — so that work is resumable, inspectable, and version-controllable without a custom database.

- Zechner's real-world example (porting Spine runtimes) keeps state in a structured porting-plan.json (metadata, deletedFiles, an ordered array of changed files each with portingState 'pending'/'done'), pre-generated deterministically by a script rather than explored by the LLM, and uses jq to update it; he cites determinism, context efficiency, and speed (seconds vs. LLM exploration).
- Zechner keeps prose conventions in ${targetRuntime}-conventions.md and a running scratch pad in porting-notes.md, enabling resumability and human checkpoints.
- Anthropic's evals post defines state and transcripts concretely: a transcript/trace/trajectory is the full record of a trial (for the Anthropic API, the messages array), and an 'outcome' is the final environment state — e.g., whether a reservation exists in a DB — not what the agent said.

# The LLM-maintained wiki: persistent knowledge bases that compile rather than retrieve

A recurring cross-source theme across several identities is the "LLM wiki" pattern: instead of uploading documents and re-deriving answers from retrieved chunks on every query (the RAG approach), an LLM incrementally builds and maintains a persistent, interlinked collection of Markdown files. Sources describe this as a compilation step at ingestion time that produces a compounding, curated knowledge artifact, and they increasingly formalize or extend the pattern. This distillation synthesizes how the pattern differs from RAG, how it is structured, and how it is being standardized and scaled.

## Compilation vs. retrieval: how the LLM wiki differs from RAG

Multiple sources contrast the LLM-wiki approach with classic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). In RAG the model retrieves relevant chunks at query time and synthesizes, 'rediscovering knowledge from scratch on every question' with no accumulation; in the LLM wiki, knowledge is compiled once at ingestion and kept current.

- Karpathy's original gist contrasts the LLM wiki with typical RAG: RAG uploads files and retrieves chunks at query time with no accumulation, whereas the LLM incrementally builds and maintains a persistent, interlinked markdown wiki sitting between the user and raw sources.
- Kunal Ganglani frames the author-coined 'Karpathy method' as treating knowledge management as 'a compilation step, not a retrieval step': RAG synthesizes at query time and is stateless per query, while the wiki synthesizes at ingestion time and is a persistent, compounding artifact with explicit Markdown cross-links and active contradiction flagging.
- Ganglani's stated tradeoff: 'RAG scales horizontally (more documents); LLM Wiki scales vertically (deeper synthesis).' He argues pure compilation does not replace production RAG for millions of documents and real-time updates, but is 'genuinely better' for individual research, architecture-decision, and reading-tracker wikis.
- Karpathy argues the key claimed difference is that the wiki is a persistent, compounding artifact where cross-references already exist, contradictions are already flagged, and the synthesis reflects everything read; the tedium of bookkeeping is why humans abandon wikis, and 'LLMs don't get bored.'
- Google Cloud's Open Knowledge Format announcement formalizes this pattern, noting developer teams are shifting to giving agents a shared markdown library ('knowledge as a living wiki') that grows more useful over time, with teams curating content and managing it like code.

Sources: [llm-wiki-github.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-github.md), [llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md), [how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing-google-cloud-blog.md](../summaries/how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing-google-cloud-blog.md)

## Structure and operations of the wiki

The sources converge on a three-layer structure and a set of recurring operations and files — raw sources, an LLM-owned wiki, and a schema/instruction document — plus index and log files that make the wiki usable at moderate scale without heavy infrastructure.

- Karpathy's architecture layers: (1) raw sources as a curated, immutable collection the LLM reads but never modifies; (2) the wiki, a directory of LLM-generated markdown files the LLM owns entirely; and (3) the schema, a document (e.g., CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) telling the LLM how the wiki is structured, its conventions, and workflows.
- Karpathy and Ganglani both describe an index.md / _index catalog of every page with a one-line summary and optional metadata, and Karpathy notes this works 'surprisingly well at moderate scale (~100 sources, ~hundreds of pages)' and avoids needing embedding-based RAG infrastructure.
- Karpathy describes log.md as a chronological, append-only record of ingests, queries, and lint passes, with consistent entry prefixes making it parseable with unix tools (e.g., grep).
- Karpathy's workflow includes Ingest (reading a new source, writing a summary page, updating the index and relevant entity/concept pages, appending to the log — a single source might touch 10–15 wiki pages), Query (searching relevant pages and synthesizing with citations, with answers filed back into the wiki as new pages), and Lint (periodic health checks for contradictions, stale claims, orphan pages, and missing cross-references).
- Ganglani's recommended Obsidian folder structure is three top-level dirs — sources/, wiki/, and _index/ (with a master-index.md he calls 'the single biggest improvement over the raw gist').

Sources: [llm-wiki-github.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-github.md), [llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md)

# The LLM Wiki Pattern: Compiling Persistent Knowledge Bases vs. Retrieving on Every Query

Two independent sources — Andrej Karpathy's GitHub gist "LLM Wiki" (an "idea file" published April 2026) and Kunal Ganglani's practitioner field report on running that pattern daily for ~3 months (April–July 2026) — describe and extend the same design pattern for personal knowledge management with LLMs. The core idea: instead of RAG-style retrieval that "rediscovers knowledge from scratch on every question," an LLM agent incrementally compiles sources into a persistent, interlinked markdown wiki, so knowledge is "compiled once and then kept current, not re-derived on every query." Karpathy supplies the abstract pattern; Ganglani supplies an honest assessment of what holds up in sustained daily use and what breaks down.

## Core idea: compile knowledge once, don't retrieve it on every query

Both sources contrast the LLM Wiki pattern with traditional RAG, where the model retrieves relevant document chunks at query time and synthesizes from scratch each time, with no accumulation. In the wiki pattern, the LLM reads each new source and integrates it into a persistent, interlinked wiki, flagging contradictions and updating cross-references and summaries. Ganglani calls this 'a compiler for knowledge, not a search engine.'

- Karpathy: 'Most people's experience with LLMs and documents looks like RAG... the LLM is rediscovering knowledge from scratch on every question. There's no accumulation.' The wiki instead is 'a persistent, compounding artifact' — 'The knowledge is compiled once and then kept current, not re-derived on every query.'
- Ganglani frames the same inversion: 'In traditional RAG... you retrieve relevant fragments at query time... Every query pays the full synthesis cost. The Karpathy method inverts this. You pay the synthesis cost once, up front, when you ingest a new source... Querying is just reading.'
- Both highlight explicit vs. implicit cross-referencing: RAG links via embedding similarity (implicit, surfaced only when retrieved), while the wiki has explicit markdown links between entity/topic pages that already exist.
- Ganglani emphasizes the ownership inversion: 'The LLM owns the wiki's structure and content. You own the sources and the questions. You become the curator and editor, not the author.' After three months his research wiki had 147 interlinked pages, zero written by hand, built from 43 sources and ~200 questions.

Sources: [llm-wiki-github.md](../llm-wiki-github.md), [llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md](../llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md)

## Architecture and how the pattern is structured

Karpathy proposes three layers: immutable raw sources, the LLM-owned wiki of markdown pages, and a schema file (e.g., CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) that tells the LLM wiki structure, conventions, and workflows. Ganglani operationalizes this with a concrete Obsidian vault layout and agent setup, and stresses the killer feature of scoped incremental updates so the pattern stays maintainable.

- Karpathy's three layers: (1) Raw sources — curated, immutable documents the LLM reads but never modifies; (2) The wiki — LLM-generated markdown summaries, entity/concept pages, comparisons, overview, synthesis, entirely LLM-written; (3) The schema — 'the key configuration file... what makes the LLM a disciplined wiki maintainer rather than a generic chatbot,' co-evolved with the user.
- Karpathy's division of labor: 'the human curates sources, directs the analysis, asks good questions, and thinks about what it all means. The LLM's job is everything else.' His central metaphor: 'Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer; the wiki is the codebase.'
- Ganglani's setup: an Obsidian vault with three top-level directories — `sources/` (raw input), `wiki/` (compiled pages, one file per entity/topic with YAML frontmatter), and `_index/` (auto-generated listings) — plus a coding agent (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, or Gemini CLI) with the Karpathy gist pasted into its system prompt. Setup takes 15 minutes, but 'getting it running well takes a few weeks of iteration.'
- Ganglani's scoped-update workflow (the pattern's 'killer feature'): drop a source into `sources/`, have the agent list affected pages without editing, review/scope that list, then instruct surgical updates ('Update only wiki/transformer-architecture.md and wiki/attention-mechanisms.md... flag any contradictions'), run a contradiction check, and review diffs via git. - Karpathy recommends `index.md` (content-oriented catalog, read first when answering queries) and `log.md` (chronological, append-only ingest/query/lint record, e.g., parseable via `grep "^## \[" log.md | tail -5`), and notes the index approach 'works surprisingly well at moderate scale (~100 sources, ~hundreds of pages) and avoids the need for embedding-based RAG infrastructure.'

# LLM-as-judge: model-based grading of AI agent outputs

A distinct cross-source theme is using an LLM as a judge or grader to evaluate output quality, in contrast to deterministic checks. Multiple sources describe LLM-as-judge scoring followed by a rubric, note the need for calibration against human experts, and advise guarding against non-determinism and hallucination in judges. This distillation gathers the shared practices and caveats around model-based evaluation.

## LLM-as-judge scoring against a rubric

Sources describe using a language model to grade responses against explicit criteria (a rubric), and treating these judges as reliable only when the rubric is well-defined and anchored with examples.

- Heltweg uses LLM-as-judge: AI agents score answers per a defined rubric, and he states that with good prompts LLMs are 'reliable judges' of response quality, but the rubrics can be adjusted when judge judgments don't match the domain expert's; he defines annotations in Markdown with definitions, rating scales, and anchor examples, using a five-point Likert scale with score plus reasoning.
- Anthropic's evals post categorizes model-based grading as rubric scoring, natural-language assertions, pairwise comparison, reference-based eval, and multi-judge consensus, and describes these as flexible, scalable, and nuanced but non-deterministic, more expensive, and requiring calibration with human graders.
- Anthropic's tools post uses a verifier 'as simple as exact string comparison or as advanced as having Claude judge responses', while cautioning against overly strict verifiers that reject valid alternative answers.
- Anthropic's evals post also stresses calibration: calibrate LLM-as-judge with human experts, give LLM judges a 'way out' (a return 'Unknown' option) to avoid hallucination, and use isolated judges per evaluation dimension.
- Osmani advocates 'LLM-as-a-Judge' for subjective acceptance criteria, alongside self-verification prompts, in his spec-writing framework.

Sources: [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md](../summaries/how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md)

## Limits and calibration of model-based judges

Sources warn that LLM judges are not perfect: they can be non-deterministic, may hallucinate, and can fail to capture expert nuance, so human calibration and domain knowledge are essential.

- Heltweg emphasizes domain knowledge is essential for good annotation: one annotation per quality dimension with clear descriptions and examples for every scale point, and notes judge judgments may not match the domain expert's, requiring rubric adjustment.
- Anthropic's evals post reports that Opus 4.5 scored 42% on CORE-Bench rising to 95% after fixing rigid grading, ambiguous specs, and irreproducible stochastic tasks — showing that judge-based and deterministic grading both carry subtle bugs.
- Anthropic's tools post notes that evaluation agents don't necessarily know correct answers, and that what agents omit can be more important than what they include ('LLMs don't always say what they mean').
- Coyle's ontology-as-guardrail proposal is an alternative/complement to judge-based scoring: instead of (or in addition to) an LLM judging quality, use a formal ontology-based validator to check that an agent's response or proposed action is reasonable before it executes.
- Anthropic's evals post describes how human studies (SME review, inter-annotator agreement) are the gold standard and should be reserved for calibrating LLM graders and evaluating subjective outputs.

Sources: [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [why-agentic-systems-need-ontologies-frank-coyle-uc-berkeley.md](../summaries/why-agentic-systems-need-ontologies-frank-coyle-uc-berkeley.md)

# The LLM-maintained wiki: persistent knowledge bases that compile rather than retrieve

A recurring cross-source theme across several identities is the "LLM wiki" pattern: instead of uploading documents and re-deriving answers from retrieved chunks on every query (the RAG approach), an LLM incrementally builds and maintains a persistent, interlinked collection of Markdown files. Sources describe this as a compilation step at ingestion time that produces a compounding, curated knowledge artifact, and they increasingly formalize or extend the pattern. This distillation synthesizes how the pattern differs from RAG, how it is structured, and how it is being standardized and scaled.

## Compilation vs. retrieval: how the LLM wiki differs from RAG

Multiple sources contrast the LLM-wiki approach with classic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). In RAG the model retrieves relevant chunks at query time and synthesizes, 'rediscovering knowledge from scratch on every question' with no accumulation; in the LLM wiki, knowledge is compiled once at ingestion and kept current.

- Karpathy's original gist contrasts the LLM wiki with typical RAG: RAG uploads files and retrieves chunks at query time with no accumulation, whereas the LLM incrementally builds and maintains a persistent, interlinked markdown wiki sitting between the user and raw sources.
- Kunal Ganglani frames the author-coined 'Karpathy method' as treating knowledge management as 'a compilation step, not a retrieval step': RAG synthesizes at query time and is stateless per query, while the wiki synthesizes at ingestion time and is a persistent, compounding artifact with explicit Markdown cross-links and active contradiction flagging.
- Ganglani's stated tradeoff: 'RAG scales horizontally (more documents); LLM Wiki scales vertically (deeper synthesis).' He argues pure compilation does not replace production RAG for millions of documents and real-time updates, but is 'genuinely better' for individual research, architecture-decision, and reading-tracker wikis.
- Karpathy argues the key claimed difference is that the wiki is a persistent, compounding artifact where cross-references already exist, contradictions are already flagged, and the synthesis reflects everything read; the tedium of bookkeeping is why humans abandon wikis, and 'LLMs don't get bored.'
- Google Cloud's Open Knowledge Format announcement formalizes this pattern, noting developer teams are shifting to giving agents a shared markdown library ('knowledge as a living wiki') that grows more useful over time, with teams curating content and managing it like code.

Sources: [llm-wiki-github.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-github.md), [llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md), [how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing-google-cloud-blog.md](../summaries/how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing-google-cloud-blog.md)

## Structure and operations of the wiki

The sources converge on a three-layer structure and a set of recurring operations and files — raw sources, an LLM-owned wiki, and a schema/instruction document — plus index and log files that make the wiki usable at moderate scale without heavy infrastructure.

- Karpathy's architecture layers: (1) raw sources as a curated, immutable collection the LLM reads but never modifies; (2) the wiki, a directory of LLM-generated markdown files the LLM owns entirely; and (3) the schema, a document (e.g., CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) telling the LLM how the wiki is structured, its conventions, and workflows.
- Karpathy and Ganglani both describe an index.md / _index catalog of every page with a one-line summary and optional metadata, and Karpathy notes this works 'surprisingly well at moderate scale (~100 sources, ~hundreds of pages)' and avoids needing embedding-based RAG infrastructure.
- Karpathy describes log.md as a chronological, append-only record of ingests, queries, and lint passes, with consistent entry prefixes making it parseable with unix tools (e.g., grep).
- Karpathy's workflow includes Ingest (reading a new source, writing a summary page, updating the index and relevant entity/concept pages, appending to the log — a single source might touch 10–15 wiki pages), Query (searching relevant pages and synthesizing with citations, with answers filed back into the wiki as new pages), and Lint (periodic health checks for contradictions, stale claims, orphan pages, and missing cross-references).
- Ganglani's recommended Obsidian folder structure is three top-level dirs — sources/, wiki/, and _index/ (with a master-index.md he calls 'the single biggest improvement over the raw gist').

Sources: [llm-wiki-github.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-github.md), [llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md)

--- the-llm-wiki-pattern-compiling-persistent-knowledge-bases-vs-retrieving-on-every-query.md
# The LLM Wiki Pattern: Compiling Persistent Knowledge Bases vs. Retrieving on Every Query

Two independent sources — Andrej Karpathy's GitHub gist "LLM Wiki" (an "idea file" published April 2026) and Kunal Ganglani's practitioner field report on running that pattern daily for ~3 months (April–July 2026) — describe and extend the same design pattern for personal knowledge management with LLMs. The core idea: instead of RAG-style retrieval that "rediscovers knowledge from scratch on every question," an LLM agent incrementally compiles sources into a persistent, interlinked markdown wiki, so knowledge is "compiled once and then kept current, not re-derived on every query." Karpathy supplies the abstract pattern; Ganglani supplies an honest assessment of what holds up in sustained daily use and what breaks down.

## Core idea: compile knowledge once, don't retrieve it on every query

Both sources contrast the LLM Wiki pattern with traditional RAG, where the model retrieves relevant document chunks at query time and synthesizes from scratch each time, with no accumulation. In the wiki pattern, the LLM reads each new source and integrates it into a persistent, interlinked wiki, flagging contradictions and updating cross-references and summaries. Ganglani calls this 'a compiler for knowledge, not a search engine.'

- Karpathy: 'Most people's experience with LLMs and documents looks like RAG... the LLM is rediscovering knowledge from scratch on every question. There's no accumulation.' The wiki instead is 'a persistent, compounding artifact' — 'The knowledge is compiled once and then kept current, not re-derived on every query.'
- Ganglani frames the same inversion: 'In traditional RAG... you retrieve relevant fragments at query time... Every query pays the full synthesis cost. The Karpathy method inverts this. You pay the synthesis cost once, up front, when you ingest a new source... Querying is just reading.'
- Both highlight explicit vs. implicit cross-referencing: RAG links via embedding similarity (implicit, surfaced only when retrieved), while the wiki has explicit markdown links between entity/topic pages that already exist.
- Ganglani emphasizes the ownership inversion: 'The LLM owns the wiki's structure and content. You own the sources and the questions. You become the curator and editor, not the author.' After three months his research wiki had 147 interlinked pages, zero written by hand, built from 43 sources and ~200 questions.

Sources: [llm-wiki-github.md](../llm-wiki-github.md), [llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md](../llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md)

## Architecture and how the pattern is structured

Karpathy proposes three layers: immutable raw sources, the LLM-owned wiki of markdown pages, and a schema file (e.g., CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) that tells the LLM wiki structure, conventions, and workflows. Ganglani operationalizes this with a concrete Obsidian vault layout and agent setup, and stresses the killer feature of scoped incremental updates so the pattern stays maintainable.

- Karpathy's three layers: (1) Raw sources — curated, immutable documents the LLM reads but never modifies; (2) The wiki — LLM-generated markdown summaries, entity/concept pages, comparisons, overview, synthesis, entirely LLM-written; (3) The schema — 'the key configuration file... what makes the LLM a disciplined wiki maintainer rather than a generic chatbot,' co-evolved with the user.
- Karpathy's division of labor: 'the human curates sources, directs the analysis, asks good questions, and thinks about what it all means. The LLM's job is everything else.' His central metaphor: 'Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer; the wiki is the codebase.'
- Ganglani's setup: an Obsidian vault with three top-level directories — `sources/` (raw input), `wiki/` (compiled pages, one file per entity/topic with YAML frontmatter), and `_index/` (auto-generated listings) — plus a coding agent (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, or Gemini CLI) with the Karpathy gist pasted into its system prompt. Setup takes 15 minutes, but 'getting it running well takes a few weeks of iteration.'
- Ganglani's scoped-update workflow (the pattern's 'killer feature'): drop a source into `sources/`, have the agent list affected pages without editing, review/scope that list, then instruct surgical updates ('Update only wiki/transformer-architecture.md and wiki/attention-mechanisms.md... flag any contradictions'), run a contradiction check, and review diffs via git. Sources: [llm-wiki-github.md](../llm-wiki-github.md), [llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md](../llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md)

# LLM-as-judge: model-based grading of AI agent outputs

A distinct cross-source theme is using an LLM as a judge or grader to evaluate output quality, in contrast to deterministic checks. Multiple sources describe LLM-as-judge scoring followed by a rubric, note the need for calibration against human experts, and advise guarding against non-determinism and hallucination in judges. This distillation gathers the shared practices and caveats around model-based evaluation.

## LLM-as-judge scoring against a rubric

Sources describe using a language model to grade responses against explicit criteria (a rubric), and treating these judges as reliable only when the rubric is well-defined and anchored with examples.

- Heltweg uses LLM-as-judge: AI agents score answers per a defined rubric, and he states that with good prompts LLMs are 'reliable judges' of response quality, but the rubrics can be adjusted when judge judgments don't match the domain expert's; he defines annotations in Markdown with definitions, rating scales, and anchor examples, using a five-point Likert scale with score plus reasoning.
- Anthropic's evals post categorizes model-based grading as rubric scoring, natural-language assertions, pairwise comparison, reference-based eval, and multi-judge consensus, and describes these as flexible, scalable, and nuanced but non-deterministic, more expensive, and requiring calibration with human graders.
- Anthropic's tools post uses a verifier 'as simple as exact string comparison or as advanced as having Claude judge responses', while cautioning against overly strict verifiers that reject valid alternative answers.
- Anthropic's evals post also stresses calibration: calibrate LLM-as-judge with human experts, give LLM judges a 'way out' (a return 'Unknown' option) to avoid hallucination, and use isolated judges per evaluation dimension.
- Osmani advocates 'LLM-as-a-Judge' for subjective acceptance criteria, alongside self-verification prompts, in his spec-writing framework.

Sources: [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md](../summaries/how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md)

## Limits and calibration of model-based judges

Sources warn that LLM judges are not perfect: they can be non-deterministic, may hallucinate, and can fail to capture expert nuance, so human calibration and domain knowledge are essential.

- Heltweg emphasizes domain knowledge is essential for good annotation: one annotation per quality dimension with clear descriptions and examples for every scale point, and notes judge judgments may not match the domain expert's, requiring rubric adjustment.
- Anthropic's evals post reports that Opus 4.5 scored 42% on CORE-Bench rising to 95% after fixing rigid grading, ambiguous specs, and irreproducible stochastic tasks — showing that judge-based and deterministic grading both carry subtle bugs.
- Anthropic's tools post notes that evaluation agents don't necessarily know correct answers, and that what agents omit can be more important than what they include ('LLMs don't always say what they mean').
- Coyle's ontology-as-guardrail proposal is an alternative/complement to judge-based scoring: instead of (or in addition to) an LLM judging quality, use a formal ontology-based validator to check that an agent's response or proposed action is reasonable before it executes.
- Anthropic's evals post describes how human studies (SME review, inter-annotator agreement) are the gold standard and should be reserved for calibrating LLM graders and evaluating subjective outputs.

Sources: [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [why-agentic-systems-need-ontologies-frank-coyle-uc-berkeley.md](../summaries/why-agentic-systems-need-ontologies-frank-coyle-uc-berkeley.md)

# Measuring AI agents: evals, baselines, and regression-style testing

A strong cross-source theme is the systematic evaluation of AI agents and workflows through evals, baselines, and regression-style testing, adapted from traditional software testing. Sources argue 'you cannot improve what you cannot measure,' recommend building offline datasets and baselines before changes, and emphasize iterating on test quality and reading transcripts rather than trusting raw scores. This distillation synthesizes the evals workflow across the sources concerned with measurement.

## Measurable baselines and regression testing for agents

Sources converge on applying a testing/measurement mindset to agents: establish a baseline, build a dataset, then continuously evaluate against it so changes or model switches do not silently regress quality.

- Heltweg's core argument adapts software regression testing to AI: 'you cannot improve what you cannot measure' — define how to measure current output quality, set a baseline, then build an automated pipeline to evaluate against that baseline continuously, catching regressions whenever you make changes or switch models.
- Heltweg distinguishes offline evaluation (a static dataset of test inputs with a fixed evaluation suite, run locally — the pragmatic starting point) from online evaluation (evaluating production traces as they arrive, flagging low quality in real time or routing for human review), which he calls 'more powerful but also more complex' and suggests layering on later.
- Anthropic's evals post distinguishes capability/quality evals ('What can this agent do well?', should start at a low pass rate as a 'hill to climb') from regression evals ('Does the agent still handle everything it used to?', should be near 100% pass), and notes capability evals with high pass rates can 'graduate' into continuously run regression suites.
- Anthropic reports teams with evals can evaluate new models in days vs. weeks, and that evals resolve ambiguity between engineers and provide baseline/regression metrics (latency, tokens, cost, error rates); an example cited is SWE-bench Verified, where LLMs progressed from 40% to >80% in a year.
- Heltweg recommends running the pipeline on every change (e.g., GitHub Actions) and comparing against a stored baseline automatically, while also cautioning to start with the local pipeline first and that 'getting your rubrics right matters more than your infrastructure.'

Sources: [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md)

## Terminology and structure of evaluation suites

Sources spell out a common vocabulary and structure for evals — tasks, trials, graders, datasets, traces, annotations — useful for building reproducible evaluation pipelines.

- Anthropic defines the core units: eval, Task (problem/test case), Trial (one attempt; multiple trials for consistency), Grader (scoring logic; a task can have multiple graders), Transcript/Trace/Trajectory (full record of a trial), Outcome (final environment state), evaluation harness (end-to-end infra), and evaluation suite (collection of tasks measuring specific capabilities).
- Heltweg uses his own matching vocabulary: Trace (a single user/AI agent chat with metadata), Dataset (multiple traces), Annotation (a human- or AI-assigned score against a quality criterion; a collection forms the evaluation suite), and Experiment (running a suite against a dataset to measure the effect of a local change).
- Both sources emphasize deterministic grading where possible and model-based grading where necessary: Anthropic's evals post categorizes graders into code-based (string match, binary tests, static analysis — fast, cheap, objective but brittle), model-based (rubrics, natural-language assertions, pairwise comparison — flexible but non-deterministic), and human (SME review, inter-annotator agreement — gold standard but expensive).
- Osmani recommends building self-checks and conformance suites into specs: self-verification prompts, 'LLM-as-a-Judge' for subjective criteria, and language-independent conformance tests, plus incorporating test plans and expected outputs into the spec.
- Heltweg keeps all rubric definitions in Markdown (definitions, rating scales, anchor examples per scale point) that can be extended without touching code, using a five-point Likert scale with a score plus explanation per response.

Sources: [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md](../summaries/how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md)

# The LLM Wiki Pattern: Compiling Persistent Knowledge Bases vs. Retrieving on Every Query

Two independent sources — Andrej Karpathy's GitHub gist "LLM Wiki" (an "idea file" published April 2026) and Kunal Ganglani's practitioner field report on running that pattern daily for ~3 months (April–July 2026) — describe and extend the same design pattern for personal knowledge management with LLMs. The core idea: instead of RAG-style retrieval that "rediscovers knowledge from scratch on every question," an LLM agent incrementally compiles sources into a persistent, interlinked markdown wiki, so knowledge is "compiled once and then kept current, not re-derived on every query." Karpathy supplies the abstract pattern; Ganglani supplies an honest assessment of what holds up in sustained daily use and what breaks down.

## Core idea: compile knowledge once, don't retrieve it on every query

Both sources contrast the LLM Wiki pattern with traditional RAG, where the model retrieves relevant document chunks at query time and synthesizes from scratch each time, with no accumulation. In the wiki pattern, the LLM reads each new source and integrates it into a persistent, interlinked wiki, flagging contradictions and updating cross-references and summaries. Ganglani calls this 'a compiler for knowledge, not a search engine.'

- Karpathy: 'Most people's experience with LLMs and documents looks like RAG... the LLM is rediscovering knowledge from scratch on every question. There's no accumulation.' The wiki instead is 'a persistent, compounding artifact' — 'The knowledge is compiled once and then kept current, not re-derived on every query.'
- Ganglani frames the same inversion: 'In traditional RAG... you retrieve relevant fragments at query time... Every query pays the full synthesis cost. The Karpathy method inverts this. You pay the synthesis cost once, up front, when you ingest a new source... Querying is just reading.'
- Both highlight explicit vs. implicit cross-referencing: RAG links via embedding similarity (implicit, surfaced only when retrieved), while the wiki has explicit markdown links between entity/topic pages that already exist.
- Ganglani emphasizes the ownership inversion: 'The LLM owns the wiki's structure and content. You own the sources and the questions. You become the curator and editor, not the author.' After three months his research wiki had 147 interlinked pages, zero written by hand, built from 43 sources and ~200 questions.

Sources: [llm-wiki-github.md](../llm-wiki-github.md), [llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md](../llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md)

## Architecture and how the pattern is structured

Karpathy proposes three layers: immutable raw sources, the LLM-owned wiki of markdown pages, and a schema file (e.g., CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) that tells the LLM wiki structure, conventions, and workflows. Ganglani operationalizes this with a concrete Obsidian vault layout and agent setup, and stresses the killer feature of scoped incremental updates so the pattern stays maintainable.

- Karpathy's three layers: (1) Raw sources — curated, immutable documents the LLM reads but never modifies; (2) The wiki — LLM-generated markdown summaries, entity/concept pages, comparisons, overview, synthesis, entirely LLM-written; (3) The schema — 'the key configuration file... what makes the LLM a disciplined wiki maintainer rather than a generic chatbot,' co-evolved with the user.
- Karpathy's division of labor: 'the human curates sources, directs the analysis, asks good questions, and thinks about what it all means. The LLM's job is everything else.' His central metaphor: 'Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer; the wiki is the codebase.'
- Ganglani's setup: an Obsidian vault with three top-level directories — `sources/` (raw input), `wiki/` (compiled pages, one file per entity/topic with YAML frontmatter), and `_index/` (auto-generated listings) — plus a coding agent (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, or Gemini CLI) with the Karpathy gist pasted into its system prompt. Setup takes 15 minutes, but 'getting it running well takes a few weeks of iteration.'
- Ganglani's scoped-update workflow (the pattern's 'killer feature'): drop a source into `sources/`, have the agent list affected pages without editing, review/scope that list, then instruct surgical updates ('Update only wiki/transformer-architecture.md and wiki/attention-mechanisms.md... flag any contradictions'), run a contradiction check, and review diffs via git. Key rule: 'never tell the agent to update the wiki without scoping which pages' — an unscoped update on a 100+ page wiki burns tokens and introduces inconsistencies.
- Karpathy recommends `index.md` (content-oriented catalog, read first when answering queries) and `log.md` (chronological, append-only ingest/query/lint record, e.g., parseable via `grep "^## \[" log.md | tail -5`), and notes the index approach 'works surprisingly well at moderate scale (~100 sources, ~hundreds of pages) and avoids the need for embedding-based RAG infrastructure.'

Sources: [llm-wiki-github.md](../llm-wiki-github.md), [llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md](../llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md)

# LLM-as-judge: model-based grading of AI agent outputs

A distinct cross-source theme is using an LLM as a judge or grader to evaluate output quality, in contrast to deterministic checks. Multiple sources describe LLM-as-judge scoring followed by a rubric, note the need for calibration against human experts, and advise guarding against non-determinism and hallucination in judges. This distillation gathers the shared practices and caveats around model-based evaluation.

## LLM-as-judge scoring against a rubric

Sources describe using a language model to grade responses against explicit criteria (a rubric), and treating these judges as reliable only when the rubric is well-defined and anchored with examples.

- Heltweg uses LLM-as-judge: AI agents score answers per a defined rubric, and he states that with good prompts LLMs are 'reliable judges' of response quality, but the rubrics can be adjusted when judge judgments don't match the domain expert's; he defines annotations in Markdown with definitions, rating scales, and anchor examples, using a five-point Likert scale with score plus reasoning.
- Anthropic's evals post categorizes model-based grading as rubric scoring, natural-language assertions, pairwise comparison, reference-based eval, and multi-judge consensus, and describes these as flexible, scalable, and nuanced but non-deterministic, more expensive, and requiring calibration with human graders.
- Anthropic's tools post uses a verifier 'as simple as exact string comparison or as advanced as having Claude judge responses', while cautioning against overly strict verifiers that reject valid alternative answers.
- Anthropic's evals post also stresses calibration: calibrate LLM-as-judge with human experts, give LLM judges a 'way out' (a return 'Unknown' option) to avoid hallucination, and use isolated judges per evaluation dimension.
- Osmani advocates 'LLM-as-a-Judge' for subjective acceptance criteria, alongside self-verification prompts, in his spec-writing framework.

Sources: [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md](../summaries/how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md)

## Limits and calibration of model-based judges

Sources warn that LLM judges are not perfect: they can be non-deterministic, may hallucinate, and can fail to capture expert nuance, so human calibration and domain knowledge are essential.

- Heltweg emphasizes domain knowledge is essential for good annotation: one annotation per quality dimension with clear descriptions and examples for every scale point, and notes judge judgments may not match the domain expert's, requiring rubric adjustment.
- Anthropic's evals post reports that Opus 4.5 scored 42% on CORE-Bench rising to 95% after fixing rigid grading, ambiguous specs, and irreproducible stochastic tasks — showing that judge-based and deterministic grading both carry subtle bugs.
- Anthropic's tools post notes that evaluation agents don't necessarily know correct answers, and that what agents omit can be more important than what they include ('LLMs don't always say what they mean').
- Coyle's ontology-as-guardrail proposal is an alternative/complement to judge-based scoring: instead of (or in addition to) an LLM judging quality, use a formal ontology-based validator to check that an agent's response or proposed action is reasonable before it executes.
- Anthropic's evals post describes how human studies (SME review, inter-annotator agreement) are the gold standard and should be reserved for calibrating LLM graders and evaluating subjective outputs.

Sources: [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/writing-effective-tools-for-ai-agents-using-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [why-agentic-systems-need-ontologies-frank-coyle-uc-berkeley.md](../summaries/why-agentic-systems-need-ontologies-frank-coyle-uc-berkeley.md)

--- measuring-ai-agents-evals-baselines-and-regression-style-testing.md
# Measuring AI agents: evals, baselines, and regression-style testing

A strong cross-source theme is the systematic evaluation of AI agents and workflows through evals, baselines, and regression-style testing, adapted from traditional software testing. Sources argue 'you cannot improve what you cannot measure,' recommend building offline datasets and baselines before changes, and emphasize iterating on test quality and reading transcripts rather than trusting raw scores. This distillation synthesizes the evals workflow across the sources concerned with measurement.

## Measurable baselines and regression testing for agents

Sources converge on applying a testing/measurement mindset to agents: establish a baseline, build a dataset, then continuously evaluate against it so changes or model switches do not silently regress quality.

- Heltweg's core argument adapts software regression testing to AI: 'you cannot improve what you cannot measure' — define how to measure current output quality, set a baseline, then build an automated pipeline to evaluate against that baseline continuously, catching regressions whenever you make changes or switch models.
- Heltweg distinguishes offline evaluation (a static dataset of test inputs with a fixed evaluation suite, run locally — the pragmatic starting point) from online evaluation (evaluating production traces as they arrive, flagging low quality in real time or routing for human review), which he calls 'more powerful but also more complex' and suggests layering on later.
- Anthropic's evals post distinguishes capability/quality evals ('What can this agent do well?', should start at a low pass rate as a 'hill to climb') from regression evals ('Does the agent still handle everything it used to?', should be near 100% pass), and notes capability evals with high pass rates can 'graduate' into continuously run regression suites.
- Anthropic reports teams with evals can evaluate new models in days vs. weeks, and that evals resolve ambiguity between engineers and provide baseline/regression metrics (latency, tokens, cost, error rates); an example cited is SWE-bench Verified, where LLMs progressed from 40% to >80% in a year.
- Heltweg recommends running the pipeline on every change (e.g., GitHub Actions) and comparing against a stored baseline automatically, while also cautioning to start with the local pipeline first and that 'getting your rubrics right matters more than your infrastructure.'

Sources: [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md)

## Terminology and structure of evaluation suites

Sources spell out a common vocabulary and structure for evals — tasks, trials, graders, datasets, traces, annotations — useful for building reproducible evaluation pipelines.

- Anthropic defines the core units: eval, Task (problem/test case), Trial (one attempt; multiple trials for consistency), Grader (scoring logic; a task can have multiple graders), Transcript/Trace/Trajectory (full record of a trial), Outcome (final environment state), evaluation harness (end-to-end infra), and evaluation suite (collection of tasks measuring specific capabilities).
- Heltweg uses his own matching vocabulary: Trace (a single user/AI agent chat with metadata), Dataset (multiple traces), Annotation (a human- or AI-assigned score against a quality criterion; a collection forms the evaluation suite), and Experiment (running a suite against a dataset to measure the effect of a local change).
- Both sources emphasize deterministic grading where possible and model-based grading where necessary: Anthropic's evals post categorizes graders into code-based (string match, binary tests, static analysis — fast, cheap, objective but brittle), model-based (rubrics, natural-language assertions, pairwise comparison — flexible but non-deterministic), and human (SME review, inter-annotator agreement — gold standard but expensive).
- Osmani recommends building self-checks and conformance suites into specs: self-verification prompts, 'LLM-as-a-Judge' for subjective criteria, and language-independent conformance tests, plus incorporating test plans and expected outputs into the spec.
- Heltweg keeps all rubric definitions in Markdown (definitions, rating scales, anchor examples per scale point) that can be extended without touching code, using a five-point Likert scale with a score plus explanation per response.

Sources: [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md), [how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md](../summaries/how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md)

--- prompts-and-specs-as-code-treating-agent-engineering-as-a-software-engineering-discipline.md
# Prompts and specs as code: treating agent engineering as a software engineering discipline

A prominent cross-source theme is that building reliable AI agents and prompt/spec systems should be treated as a software engineering discipline rather than ad hoc experimentation. Several sources converge on treating prompts and specifications as code, structuring files (JSON for structured data, Markdown for prose) as durable state, and version-controlling specifications and workflows. This distillation captures the framing, the file-based state pattern, iterative maintenance, and the limits acknowledged by the authors.

## Prompts and specs as code, executed on an unreliable computer

Multiple authors reframe writing prompts for LLM coding agents as a form of 'metaprogramming' or engineering practice, mapping traditional software concepts onto prompt-driven execution so that behavior becomes deterministic and revisable.

- Mario Zechner's core thesis is that 'agentic engineering' is usually ad hoc experimentation; he recommends treating LLMs as 'an extremely slow kind of unreliable computer that we program with natural language,' mapping Program = the prompt, Inputs = prepared info/user input/tool outputs, State = data serialized to disk (JSON for structured data via jq, Markdown for unstructured), and Outputs = generated code/diffs/summaries.
- Addy Osmani frames a good AI-agent spec as a 'source of truth' document that should be a living, version-controlled artifact and an 'executable artifact' integrated into toolchains, blending PRD and SRS mindsets.
- Osmani argues agents need context broken into modular prompts rather than one giant prompt, citing the 'curse of instructions' — research that piling more instructions into a prompt drops model adherence — and recommends dividing specs into phases/components with per-section summaries as a hierarchical index.
- Karpathy's schema layer (e.g., CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md) plays the analogous role of a config/instruction file that makes a language model a 'disciplined maintainer rather than a generic chatbot', and he describes it as co-evolved over time.
- Anthropic's evals post makes the same engineering-discipline point at the team level: teams without evals stay in reactive debugging loops, and rigorous evals become necessary once agents scale and 'fly blind'.

Sources: [prompts-are-code-json-md-files-are-state.md](../summaries/prompts-are-code-json-md-files-are-state.md), [how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md](../summaries/how-to-write-a-good-spec-for-ai-agents-by-addy-osmani.md), [llm-wiki-github.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-github.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md)

## Files as state: JSON and Markdown as the durable medium

A consistent implementation pattern across sources is persisting state and knowledge in plain files — structured data in JSON, prose in Markdown — so that work is resumable, inspectable, and version-controllable without a custom database.

- Zechner's real-world example (porting Spine runtimes) keeps state in a structured porting-plan.json (metadata, deletedFiles, an ordered array of changed files each with portingState 'pending'/'done'), pre-generated deterministically by a script rather than explored by the LLM, and uses jq to update it; he cites determinism, context efficiency, and speed (seconds vs. LLM exploration).
- Zechner keeps prose conventions in ${targetRuntime}-conventions.md and a running scratch pad in porting-notes.md, enabling resumability and human checkpoints.
- Anthropic's evals post defines state and transcripts concretely: a transcript/trace/trajectory is the full record of a trial (for the Anthropic API, the messages array), and an 'outcome' is the final environment state — e.g., whether a reservation exists in a DB — not what the agent said.
- Karpathy's wiki, Ganglani's setup, and Google Cloud's OKF all model knowledge as markdown files (plus YAML frontmatter) inside a git repo, giving version history, branching, and collaboration for free; OKF calls this 'just files (tarball/git-repo/filesystem)'.
- Heltweg stores evaluation traces as human-readable Markdown files with YAML frontmatter ending with the last user message, loaded in Python via a provided load_scenarios function — the same file-based pattern applied to evaluation.

Sources: [prompts-are-code-json-md-files-are-state.md](../summaries/prompts-are-code-json-md-files-are-state.md), [demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md](../summaries/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents-anthropic.md), [llm-wiki-github.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-github.md), [how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing-google-cloud-blog.md](../summaries/how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing-google-cloud-blog.md), [structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md](../summaries/structured-evaluation-pipelines-to-improve-your-ai-workflows-philip-heltweg.md)

# The LLM-maintained wiki: persistent knowledge bases that compile rather than retrieve

A recurring cross-source theme across several identities is the "LLM wiki" pattern: instead of uploading documents and re-deriving answers from retrieved chunks on every query (the RAG approach), an LLM incrementally builds and maintains a persistent, interlinked collection of Markdown files. Sources describe this as a compilation step at ingestion time that produces a compounding, curated knowledge artifact, and they increasingly formalize or extend the pattern. This distillation synthesizes how the pattern differs from RAG, how it is structured, and how it is being standardized and scaled.

## Compilation vs. retrieval: how the LLM wiki differs from RAG

Multiple sources contrast the LLM-wiki approach with classic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). In RAG the model retrieves relevant chunks at query time and synthesizes, 'rediscovering knowledge from scratch on every question' with no accumulation; in the LLM wiki, knowledge is compiled once at ingestion and kept current.

- Karpathy's original gist contrasts the LLM wiki with typical RAG: RAG uploads files and retrieves chunks at query time with no accumulation, whereas the LLM incrementally builds and maintains a persistent, interlinked markdown wiki sitting between the user and raw sources.
- Kunal Ganglani frames the author-coined 'Karpathy method' as treating knowledge management as 'a compilation step, not a retrieval step': RAG synthesizes at query time and is stateless per query, while the wiki synthesizes at ingestion time and is a persistent, compounding artifact with explicit Markdown cross-links and active contradiction flagging.
- Ganglani's stated tradeoff: 'RAG scales horizontally (more documents); LLM Wiki scales vertically (deeper synthesis).' He argues pure compilation does not replace production RAG for millions of documents and real-time updates, but is 'genuinely better' for individual research, architecture-decision, and reading-tracker wikis.
- Karpathy argues the key claimed difference is that the wiki is a persistent, compounding artifact where cross-references already exist, contradictions are already flagged, and the synthesis reflects everything read; the tedium of bookkeeping is why humans abandon wikis, and 'LLMs don't get bored.'
- Google Cloud's Open Knowledge Format announcement formalizes this pattern, noting developer teams are shifting to giving agents a shared markdown library ('knowledge as a living wiki') that grows more useful over time, with teams curating content and managing it like code.

Sources: [llm-wiki-github.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-github.md), [llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md](../summaries/llm-wiki-setup-karpathy-s-knowledge-base-2026-guide.md), [how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing-google-cloud-blog.md](../summaries/how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing-google-cloud-blog.md)

      "markdown": "How to write a good spec for AI agents - by Addy Osmani . How to structure, plan, and iterate for high-performance coding agents . Start with a high-level vision and let the AI draft the details .\n"

      "raw_written_at": "2026-09-01T08:27:17.608854+00:00",
      "markdown": "The Open Knowledge Format (OKF) is an open specification that formalizes the [LLM-Wiki] pattern into a portable, interoperable format . This is a vendor-neutral, agent- and human-friendly standard for representing metadata, context, and curated knowledge that modern AI systems need .       "raw_written_at": "2026-09-01T08:27:21.146951+00:00",
      "markdown": "An idea file is designed to be copy pasted to your own LLM Agent (e.g. OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode / Pi, or etc.) Its goal is to communicate the high level idea, but your agent will build out the specifics in collaboration with you . Instead of just retrieving from raw documents at query time, the LLM builds and maintains a persistent wiki .\n"

    {

      "markdown": "Philip Heltweg: Structured Evaluation Pipelines to improve the quality of AI workflows .       "markdown": "Using Claude Code, Claude Code is a way to engineer software that's hard to maintain, hard to understand, and full of places for bugs to hide .       "raw_written_at": "2026-09-01T08:27:24.159175+00:00",
      "markdown": "Architecture for Building Readable, Robust, and Extensible Apps . Layered architecture separates responsibilities and keeps business logic independent of frameworks and infrastructure . Application layers orchestrate workflows; domain layers define meaning and constraints . The outer layer can be split in two sides: input side, output side, repository and infrastructure layers, which may communicate with external systems such as API, database and message queues . content.text:
Yes. The sidecar run passed operational checks, but summary quality was materially worse.

Comparison uses the two preceding successful end-to-end reports, with the same 16-source corpus and `deepseek-v4-pro` evaluator:

| Stage | Sidecar | Prior mean | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Summarize | 2.578/5 | 4.961/5 | −2.383, −48.0% |
| Distill | 4.240/5 | 4.900/5 | −0.660, −13.5% |

Summary metric losses:

- Coverage: 1.312 vs 4.969 (−3.657)
- Faithfulness: 2.938 vs 4.938 (−2.000)
- Usefulness: 1.750 vs 5.000 (−3.250)
- Page cleanliness: 4.312 vs 4.938 (−0.626)

Manual inspection explains the result:

- Sidecar summaries are single paragraphs, 247–752 characters each; median length is 356 characters.
- Prior summaries are structured Markdown, typically 3,000–12,000 characters.
- All 16 sidecar summaries scored usefulness 1–3; coverage was 1 for 11 documents and 2 for 5.
- Several outputs contain factual errors or omit nearly all source detail. For example, the architecture summary says the application layer calls into itself, and the Phi-4 summary misstates where the model is available.
- Distill documents remain usable, but the comparison is directional because the runs produced different counts: 5 sidecar documents versus 1 and 4 in the prior runs.

Reports: [sidecar]( /Users/simon/projects/bo/evals/results/end-to-end-1788251237-50409/evaluation/aggregate.json), [prior run 1]( /Users/simon/projects/bo/evals/results/end-to-end-1788016442-36303/evaluation/aggregate.json), [prior run 2]( /Users/simon/projects/bo/evals/results/end-to-end-1788074878-97888/evaluation/aggregate.json).

Conclusion: the integration works, but `distilbart-cnn-12-6` output is not acceptable for production-quality summaries without stronger generation controls or post-processing.

Weak summaries can still hurt even with raw access:

- They guide theme discovery and source selection.
- They hide relationships, so the model may never request the correct raw files.
- They reduce the useful context available before tool calls.
- Incorrect compressed claims can propagate unless the model rechecks them against raw evidence.

The observed pattern supports this: summary quality fell about 48%, while distillation fell about 13.5%. Cross-source integration dropped most, by 1.2 points, followed by structure and usefulness at 0.8 points each. Attribution stayed high because the write path enforces provenance.

1. sidecar summaries with summary-only tools;
2. the same sidecar summaries with the full raw-reading tool set and a larger timeout;
3. optionally, existing DeepSeek summaries with summary-only tools.

That will show whether the remaining loss comes mostly from lossy summaries or from removing raw retrieval.
